items.title: UK GDPR, Article 22A: Automated processing and significant decisions
items.quote: a person must consider, among other things, the extent to which the decision is reached by means of profiling
items.why: Source of the quotation and the binding definition of both scoping tests. A decision is significant if it produces a legal effect or a similarly significant effect; solely automated if there is no meaningful human involvement. Inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, s.80; in force 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82, reg. 2(j)). The statute does not define 'meaningful'.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 22D: Further provision about automated decision-making
items.quote: a description of decision is, or is not, to be taken to have a similarly significant effect for the data subject
items.why: The Secretary of State may say by regulation when human involvement is or is not meaningful and which decisions do or do not have a similarly significant effect (affirmative procedure). Any scoping conclusion can therefore be changed by regulation. No such regulations were found on legislation.gov.uk on the date checked.

items.title: Automated decision-making, including profiling: What does the UK GDPR say about ADM?
items.locator: Sections 'When do the ADM provisions apply?', 'What is a 'significant decision'?' and 'What is a 'solely' automated decision?'
items.quote: You should keep a record of how the human was involved in the decision.
items.why: Consultation draft (updated 31 March 2026), not final guidance. Source of the figure: the provisions apply only when three factors are present. Lists the areas of a person's life to weigh for significance, five criteria for meaningful involvement applied to every decision, and says spot checks are not sufficient and involvement must come before the decision is applied.

items.title: Automated decision-making, including profiling: What else do we need to consider?
items.locator: Section 'Do we have to do a data protection impact assessment (DPIA)?'
items.quote: A DPIA can help you decide whether or not the ADM provisions are likely to apply to your intended processing in the first place.
items.why: Consultation draft, not final guidance. Places the scoping question inside the impact assessment, which UK GDPR Article 35(3)(a) requires for systematic and extensive automated evaluation leading to significant decisions. Gives the scoping record a natural home.

items.title: Recruitment rewired: Meaningful human involvement
items.locator: Section 'Our findings about meaningful human involvement'
items.quote: However, the evidence we saw indicated that, in practice, employers were using the tools to make solely automated decisions.
items.why: What mis-scoping looks like in practice: most employers classed their tools as decision support, but hiring managers were unlikely to review lower-scoring candidates. Also says design-stage human input does not count. Recruitment only; the regulator's view, not a court ruling.

items.title: Recruitment rewired: Understanding how meaningful human involvement applies: use cases
items.locator: Use cases 'tools used to provide 'fit' scores' and 'mandatory screening questions'
items.quote: This means that a human must make every decision about whether to progress a candidate to the next stage.
items.why: Worked examples of the boundary. Automatic rejection below a pass mark is in scope; so is manual rejection where the manager does not consider every application. A yes/no screening question set by a human in advance is not, because the tool only applies a predetermined rule.

items.title: Recruitment rewired: DPIAs
items.locator: Sections 'Our findings about DPIAs' and case study
items.quote: This is not compliant, because the employer hasn’t fully assessed the extent to which its processing is within the scope of the ADM provisions.
items.why: The regulator treats an unanswered scope question as a compliance failure in itself: in its case study an impact assessment recorded the scope question as unsure with no reasoning. Supports keeping the reasoning, not only the conclusion.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 30: Records of processing activities
items.quote: The records referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 shall be in writing, including in electronic form.
items.why: The statutory register that a scoping record can be linked to, and which the regulator can ask to see. Article 30 does not itself require a note of whether a decision is solely automated; linking the two is good practice, not a legal duty.

items.title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) Mandatory Scope and Exemptions Policy
items.locator: Section 4.2 'For which tools must I complete an algorithmic transparency record?'
items.quote: ‘Significant influence’ includes where an algorithmic tool meaningfully assists, supplements, or fully automates a decision-making process.
items.why: A second UK scoping test, for central government only. It is wider than the data protection one: tools that assist a decision are in scope, not only those that decide alone. Shows that a system outside the automated-decision rules may still fall inside another regime. GOV.UK marks the page as published under the 2024 to 2026 government; check for a successor before relying on it.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Annex III: High-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2)
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: AI systems intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score
items.why: Comparator only. The Commission's copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned an empty page). The EU scopes by listed use (recruitment, credit scoring, benefits and others) whether or not a human is involved, unlike the UK test. The page showed no amendment notice on the date checked, though other pages on the same site say the Act was amended by the Digital Omnibus; no application date is given in the brief.

items.title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025: Explanatory Notes
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and other departments (legislation.gov.uk)
items.locator: Commentary on section 80, paras 634 to 645 (PDF pp. 84-85); quote at para 644
items.quote: clarify when meaningful human involvement can be said to have taken place in light of constantly emerging technologies
items.why: The government's own account of the two scoping tests and of why ministers took power to redefine them: the meaningful-involvement power is tied to emerging technology, the significance power to 'changing societal expectations'. This is the rule-change a board would need to track. Limits: explanatory notes are not law and were not endorsed by Parliament; they describe the Act as passed in June 2025 and say nothing about whether regulations have been made. The PDF text has stray spaces in places; the quoted passage is clean.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 50A: Automated processing and significant decisions
items.quote: it produces an adverse legal effect for the data subject
items.why: The parallel scoping test for law enforcement processing (Part 3). Same meaningful-involvement wording as UK GDPR Article 22A, but a decision is significant only if its legal or similar effect is adverse. An organisation processing under both regimes needs two scoping tests, not one. Limits: applies only to competent authorities processing for law enforcement purposes. Substituted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.80(3), fully in force 5 February 2026 (note F1). The page lists one outstanding effect from a Northern Ireland Act not yet applied to the text.

items.title: Guidelines on Automated individual decision-making and Profiling for the purposes of Regulation 2016/679 (WP251rev.01)
items.publisher: Article 29 Data Protection Working Party (endorsed by the European Data Protection Board)
items.locator: Chapter IV, section A 'Decision based solely on automated processing', pp. 20-21; section B on 'legal' or 'similarly significant' effects, pp. 21-22
items.quote: The controller cannot avoid the Article 22 provisions by fabricating human involvement.
items.why: The European regulators' test for 'solely', which the UK draft guidance follows closely: oversight must be meaningful, not a token gesture, and done by someone with authority and competence to change the decision. It also says the degree of human involvement should be identified and recorded in the impact assessment. Limits: EU guidance on the EU GDPR's Article 22, not binding in the UK and written before Articles 22A to 22D replaced Article 22 here. Already used by another brief in this domain for a different passage (p. 27).

items.title: Human-AI Interactions in Public Sector Decision Making: 'Automation Bias' and 'Selective Adherence' to Algorithmic Advice
items.publisher: Saar Alon-Barkat and Madalina Busuioc, Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory (authors' copy on arXiv)
items.quote: We find a stronger propensity for adherence when the advice is aligned with group stereotypes
items.why: Peer-reviewed experimental evidence on what a human reviewer actually adds, which is the question the meaningful-involvement test turns on. The result is mixed and should be reported as such: the studies did not find reviewers deferring more to an algorithm than to a human expert, but did find reviewers more likely to follow advice that matched stereotypes (not repeated in the third study, of civil servants). Limits: Dutch samples and hypothetical vignettes, not live decisions; read on arXiv because the publisher's page refused a plain request.

items.title: Rethinking Decisions under Article 22 of the GDPR: Implications for Semi-Automated Legal Decision-Making
items.publisher: Peter Alexander Earls Davis and Sebastian Felix Schwemer, Proceedings of LegalAIIA 2023 (CEUR Workshop Proceedings vol. 3423)
items.locator: Abstract, p. 1; sections 3 and 4 on locating the decision
items.quote: it should be construed broadly to include recommendations or other measures leading to a particular outcome for an individual
items.why: Speaks to the first step of scoping: which step in a multi-stage process is 'the decision'. The authors argue a score or recommendation that leads to an outcome can itself be the decision, so putting a human at the end does not take a system out of scope. Limits: a workshop paper, open access on the proceedings site, lightly reviewed; it interprets the EU GDPR and relies on an Advocate General's opinion in the SCHUFA case, not the final judgment, which could not be read from an official source in this pass. Not UK law.

items.title: The flaws of policies requiring human oversight of government algorithms
items.publisher: Ben Green, Computer Law & Security Review 45 (author's copy on arXiv)
items.quote: evidence suggests that people are unable to perform the desired oversight functions
items.why: Peer-reviewed review of 41 human-oversight policies. It supports reading the answer 'a human is always involved' with caution: naming a reviewer does not show the reviewer can change outcomes. Limits: about government algorithms, mostly outside the UK; only the abstract is on the linked page; read on arXiv. Used by another brief (human oversight) for a different sentence.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Table 2, MAP 3.5 (p. 26); see also Table 1, GOVERN 3.2 (p. 22)
items.quote: Processes for human oversight are defined, assessed, and documented in accordance with organizational policies from the GOVERN function.
items.why: International comparator and the only free standard found that bears on this point. It asks for what the scoping record needs: human oversight defined, assessed and written down system by system. Limits: a voluntary United States framework; it does not use the UK legal tests of 'significant' or 'solely automated' and is not law here.
